analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA safety review before food companies can self-certify additives as safe.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee on December 4, 2023, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current rules, a food company can decide on its own that a new ingredient is 'generally recognized as safe' and put it in food without ever telling the FDA. This bill would end that self-certification: companies would have to submit their safety evidence to the FDA, the agency would post it publicly for a 90-day review, and ingredients known to cause cancer or reproductive harm could not qualify as safe. It would also create an FDA office that must re-examine at least 10 existing food chemicals every three years.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats packaged or processed food, especially the groups the bill names as most vulnerable: infants, children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, older adults, and people with preexisting conditions. They gain stronger government review of food chemicals and public access to the safety data companies currently keep to themselves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers, especially children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Ends the practice of manufacturers marketing substances as GRAS without any FDA determination; the Secretary must review the manufacturer's notice and supporting data in writing before a substance can be sold in food [S3].

Bars substances identified by the National Toxicology Program as causing cancer or reproductive or developmental toxicity from being treated as GRAS, and requires safety data accounting for vulnerable populations like infants and pregnant women [S3].
Requires the FDA to post each company's safety determination and supporting information publicly, with at least a 90-day window for the agency and the public to object [S3].
Requires standards prohibiting conflicts of interest among the experts providing safety data, strengthening the FDA's 2022 guidance on convening GRAS review panels [S3].

Creates an Office of Food Chemical Safety, Dietary Supplements, and Innovation that must reassess the safety of at least 10 food substances or classes every three years and issue regulations declaring them safe or unsafe [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage manufacturers and food-chemical suppliers, who would face mandatory FDA review before using new ingredients, public disclosure of their safety submissions, potential removal of chemicals now on the market, and the cost of re-testing and reformulating products.

drawbacks.text: Requiring written FDA sign-off on every GRAS determination would add review time and cost for food companies, which could slow the introduction of new products and ingredients [S3].

The bill directs the FDA to reassess chemicals using safety factors for vulnerable populations and to treat substances with 'some evidence' of reproductive toxicity as unsafe, which industry groups generally argue relies on preliminary science that could remove widely used ingredients; the bill text does not include a phase-in timeline for substances that fail reassessment [S3].

The bill creates significant new FDA workload — an annual compliance-monitoring plan, a standing science committee, and reassessment of at least 10 substances every three years — without any dedicated funding mechanism in the text, so its effectiveness would depend on Congress appropriating resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is stronger, more transparent safety review of chemicals in the food supply, with explicit protections for children and pregnant women; the cost is compliance burdens on food manufacturers and a heavier FDA workload that the bill does not fund. The tradeoff is real but modest: the current system lets companies certify their own ingredients' safety without notifying the FDA, which is widely considered a gap in oversight. The bill's substance is broad but its design leaves the funding question open.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on December 4, 2023, joined by three Democratic cosponsors, all from the Senate's Democratic caucus [S1].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and beverage manufacturers and food-chemical suppliers are better off: the current self-certification system, in which a company can declare an ingredient safe without FDA review, remains in place. The FDA's 2016 GRAS rule that the bill sought to revise is unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral in a chamber where Democrats held a narrow majority.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to self-certify new ingredients as GRAS without FDA review, forcing them to submit safety data publicly and potentially reformulate products. Consumers currently absorb the risk of unreviewed food chemicals.

Ingredients identified by the National Toxicology Program as carcinogenic or toxic to reproduction could no longer be sold as GRAS, and existing chemicals would face mandatory reassessment every three years, threatening established sales.
The bill requires conflict-of-interest standards for the hired experts who certify ingredients as safe, curbing a paid-review business that operates with little oversight today.
